strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and understudied problem: mechanistically understanding how vision-language models acquire and represent spatial relations (specifically, left-right symmetry).
The proposed 1D image-text toy testbed is elegant, controllable, and allows for clean, unambiguous mechanistic analysis that would be impossible in complex real-world datasets.

The attention logit decomposition is theoretically sound and empirically validated. The identification of the positional-token cross-term (the EP term) as the driver of the attention gradient is compelling and backed by clean ablation experiments.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear figures, rigorous math, and a thorough exploration of modern position encoding schemes (like RoPE) in the appendix, showing that the findings generalize beyond simple learnable absolute position embeddings.
weaknesses: The study is restricted to synthetic 1D datasets and simplified, small-scale models. While this is standard and necessary for mechanistic interpretability, there remains a gap between these findings and 2D vision-language models trained on complex natural datasets.

It is unclear how well the proposed attention gradient mechanism scales to deep multi-layer models where attention interactions are highly non-linear, though the authors provide some initial 2-layer experiments in the appendix.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and understudied problem: the mechanistic understanding of how spatial relations are learned and represented in vision-language models.
The proposed 1D synthetic testbed is simple yet elegant, allowing for clean, controlled experiments and precise isolation of causal factors.

The mechanistic analysis is exceptionally rigorous, decomposing attention logits into distinct token-position interaction terms (EE, EP, PE, PP) and validating their roles through selective inference-time ablations.

The theoretical extension to Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) is highly insightful and relevant to modern model designs, demonstrating how subspace alignment and bias-induced gradients can break symmetry.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, with clear explanations, logical flow, and highly illustrative figures.
weaknesses: The experiments are restricted to a simplified 1D synthetic setting. While this simplification is necessary and justified for a mechanistic analysis, it remains unclear to what extent these specific attention-gradient mechanisms scale up or translate to real-world 2D image models.
There is no validation or probing of pretrained, large-scale CLIP models to see if similar attention gradients (either horizontal or vertical) can be observed when processing spatial queries.

The single-layer text encoder used in the main setup has very limited capacity, requiring architectural modifications (adding a second layer) when both left and right textual representations coexist, which slightly complicates the simplicity of the analyzed system.

strengths: Provides a mathematically rigorous decomposition of attention logits into token-token (EE), token-position (EP), position-token (PE), and position-position (PP) terms to precisely isolate the mechanism of left-right symmetry breaking.

Causally verifies the theoretical claims through inference-time ablation studies, demonstrating that zeroing out the identified EP term degrades the spatial relational performance to random guess while maintaining object recognition capabilities.

Includes a thorough and impressive extension to Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), theoretically proposing and empirically validating two distinct mechanisms (bias-induced gradient and learned subspace alignment) for out-of-distribution generalization.
Systematically analyzes different types of generalization (single-object, seen-pair, and unseen-pair) and documents their sequential emergence over training epochs.
weaknesses: The 1D synthetic setup with extremely short sequence lengths (D=10) and simple object representations is highly idealized. It is unclear if horizontal attention gradients play a similarly dominant role in complex 2D spatial environments with natural imagery.

The mechanistic analysis is heavily reliant on single-layer simplifications. When scaling to a 2-layer encoder (which is shown to be necessary to handle dual left-right representations), the authors resort to leaving the detailed analysis to future work due to complexity.

The paper is diagnostic and offers few actionable strategies, architectural modifications, or training interventions to mitigate the known spatial reasoning deficiencies in state-of-the-art, large-scale vision-language models.

strengths: Highly rigorous and precise mechanistic interpretability analysis, decomposing pre-softmax attention logits into mathematically interpretable components (EE, EP, PE, PP) to locate the exact cause of spatial learning.

Remarkable thoroughness in exploring extensions, including analytical and empirical treatments of Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), multi-object scenarios, 2D images, and decoder-only autoregressive VLMs.
Insightful findings on data curriculum, demonstrating that label diversity is a much stronger driver of spatial generalization than layout diversity in contrastive setups.
Excellent presentation with exceptionally clear schematic diagrams, detailed attention maps, and intuitive visualizations that make complex attention decompositions easy to follow.
weaknesses: The study is primarily conducted within a highly simplified synthetic 1D/2D testbed. While necessary for clean mechanistic interpretability, there remains a substantial gap between these toy settings and real-world web-scale VLMs operating on complex natural scenes.

The exact mathematical decomposition relies on a simplified 1-layer, attention-only architecture. Although the authors propose an approximate decomposition for LayerNorm in the appendix, scaling this mechanistic understanding to deep, multi-layer, highly non-linear networks remains a challenge.

strengths: Provides a highly rigorous and structured mechanistic interpretability approach to a critical problem (spatial reasoning) in vision-language models, bridging a gap in the literature.

Causally validates the proposed mechanism by surgically ablating specific positional-token embedding components (the EP term) during inference, demonstrating a drop to chance level for spatial relationships while preserving object classification.
Proactively addresses potential limitations of the 1D toy setup by extending findings to 2D images, 3-object scenes, autoregressive VLMs, and models using Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE).

Presents a comprehensive mathematical analysis of how both learnable positional embeddings and RoPE break left-right symmetry, identifying elegant mechanisms like bias-induced gradients and learned subspace alignment.
weaknesses: The datasets and settings remain highly synthetic and toy-scale (e.g., 1D grids, 4x4 2D grids). It remains an open challenge to confirm whether these clean, low-dimensional positional attention gradients are the primary driver of spatial reasoning in web-scale, multi-layer VLMs.

The analysis of deep, non-linear networks remains limited. As the authors note, adding even a second layer to the text encoder to support bidirectional text representations dramatically increases the complexity of interpreting how spatial structures are resolved.
The syntactic and semantic templates for text captions are extremely simplified, which avoids the natural linguistic noise and ambiguity present in real-world training data.

strengths: Provides an outstanding mechanistic insight into how Transformer-based vision-language models encode spatial relations by decomposing the attention logits into interpretable components.

Demonstrates exceptional methodological rigor with clean causal interventions, such as ablating the positional-token (EP) cross-term during inference to show it specifically degrades relative spatial ordering while leaving object recognition intact.
Extends the toy 1D analysis thoroughly to more complex settings in the appendix, including 2D grids, 3-object scenes, Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), and autoregressive VLM architectures.
Proposes a novel approximate attention decomposition for LayerNorm, which helps bridge the gap between simplified attention-only models and real-world non-linear networks.
Reveals a counter-intuitive and highly useful data insight: label diversity is a much stronger driver of spatial generalization than layout diversity in this setting.
weaknesses: The experimental setup remains restricted to low-dimensional synthetic testbeds (1D and 4x4 2D grids). While appropriate for mechanistic interpretability, further work is required to fully bridge this to natural, complex real-world images.

While the paper successfully diagnoses the mechanistic pathway for spatial understanding, it does not propose a concrete, actionable training recipe or architectural modification to solve spatial reasoning failures in state-of-the-art web-scale VLMs.
